properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. @ajs, 2026-10-10, dev_reflow2 hub session: "This is almost like we are pushing 'hub' operations down to reflow2 and down to keys:values level (can't go much lower). So far reflow2's operations have focused on a single design graph. I think what I'm describing is another layer of primitives in reflow2 that now allow comparison, splicing, merging (on demand), and some other basic database level operations between two or more designs within the same reflow2 db. I think flo2 would handle who can access who's designs. I think there are some benefits to bringing things down to the lowest level. Things should be able to be done ultra fast (rocksdb has some other features that may already do some of these operations at the db level, so may be worth doing some research). Secondly, it removes having the AI agent have to read two or more designs, determine what's different, then make design changes appropriately. This, I think would change the order of operations to, reflow2 doing all the comparison ops at the db level, and returning the results to the agent."

WHAT IS TRUE TODAY (measured in the code, 2026-10-10):
- There is no "same reflow2 db": each design is its own RocksDB instance (one store per folder; no column families used). What is shared is the PROCESS: the registry (cap:graph-registry) holds many DesignGraphs open at once, by graph_id, opened on demand and evicted when idle. On flo2.io that one process holds every hosted design.
- The cross-design operations largely EXIST, engine-side, returning results rather than designs: compare_designs (a diff), merge_designs (three-way, cap:merge-designs), fork_point, compose_and_analyse (req:composed-analysis: assemble under namespaces, run the ordinary checks), pair_designs and seam_coverage (cap:complementary-pairing, cap:seam-incompatibility), and since 0.81.0 send/receive between designs and typed xref references. Each takes its second design BY PATH, so a hosted server withholds them, and each runs on one pair.
- So the gap is not the operations and not the storage: it is that nothing serves them BY GRAPH_ID over the designs one process already holds, N at a time, under the host's membership filter. Today's accepted intent already asks for the results of that (req:two-or-more-designs-are-compared-on-one-topic-on-demand, req:a-composed-analysis-across-a-familys-designs-writes-its-seam-gaps-back-to-the-hub, req:a-design-takes-a-chunk-of-another-as-copies-with-provenance-and-a-watch, flo2's req:flo2-io-assembles-a-hubs-designs-into-one-graph-when-asked); this idea names the layer they would share.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN:
(a) A CROSS-DESIGN LAYER IN THE REGISTRY: every operation that today takes a second design by path also takes graph_ids, resolved to the stores the process holds (opening on demand), with the caller's allowed set passed in by the host (flo2's gateway already knows membership). compare, compose, merge, fork_point, topic compare, chunk take, seam gaps: one family, one permission check, results returned. MEDIUM: a resolver from graph_id to an open DesignGraph for a second (or Nth) design, the read-lock discipline across two stores, and the host handing the allowed set. No storage change.
(b) ONE RocksDB WITH A COLUMN FAMILY PER DESIGN: designs share one DB; db-level snapshots, one block cache, atomic batches across designs become possible. It is the stored union he set aside an hour ago in different clothes: one file set, one lock, one backup, one blast radius for N designs; and a column family is still a separate key space, so a cross-design compare is no cheaper than across two DBs in one process. LARGE, and it reopens three settlements.
(c) RocksDB FEATURES AS SPEED-UPS UNDER (a), research first: checkpoints (a cheap consistent copy of a store for an assembly or a backup without stopping the engine, which flo2's nightly backup stops it for today), SST ingestion (a chunk or a whole design spliced in as files rather than key by key), a block cache shared across the stores one process holds. SMALL to research; each is a later optimization of (a), not a prerequisite.
(d) AS TODAY: the agent reads both designs and works out the difference in its own context, which is what the StoryFlow session did this evening.

PUSHBACK, KEPT BESIDE IT:
- "ULTRA FAST" IS BOUNDED BY OPENING, NOT BY KEY SCANS. Measured today: 0.3 s to open a small design, 8 to 11 s for reflow2's own; a key:value scan of either is milliseconds. In one process that already holds the designs (flo2.io) the open cost is paid once and (a) is fast; locally, each design is opened by path as now.
- KEY EQUALITY IS NOT DESIGN EQUALITY. Two designs name the same thing with different ids and words; a db-level compare finds only what shares an id (useful for forks, which fork_point and merge_designs serve) and nothing for flo2's OAuth against StoryFlow's. The cross-vocabulary half is similarity scoring (the duplicate guard, the family check: one true duplicate in eight at 0.4), which is CPU over text, not a db operation, and whose output is candidates for a judgement. The order of operations he wants holds for the engine finding and ranking; the deciding stays with the agent or the person.
- THE HOST OWNS "WHO MAY READ WHAT", and must pass the allowed set on every cross-design call; an answer must leave out an unreadable design and say so without saying what it held.
- A MERGE ACROSS DESIGNS IS A WRITE, and the single-writer lock is per store; (a) must take two write locks in a fixed order or refuse, or it deadlocks the registry.
- CHEAPEST REAL STEP: (a)'s resolver, with compare_designs and compose_and_analyse as the first two tools to take graph_ids, measured on flo2.io's registry before anything else is widened.

LATER THE SAME EVENING, @ajs, thinking out loud (recorded as an idea, in his words, not as intent): "I think this could be pretty revolutionary for how a 'hub' or 'project-brain' is done within the whole integrated-flo system of systems design. Having an 'on-demand' of here is the 'one graph', which is not much more than a cache stored set of key:value (design A) + key:value (design B) + ... + key:value (design N) that can allow the agent to basically treat them as 'one graph' and do all the other basic reflow2 skills tools on this 'one graph'... then when done with the operation, the agent can just release the 'one design' and any changes stay within their respective designs of design A, B.... N. maybe I'm over playing this, but I think it is pretty cool."

WHAT THIS ADDS TO (a): not a new operation but a VIEW. (a) as written serves named operations (compare, compose, merge...) by graph_id; this says the ordinary tool set — search, detect_gaps, propagate_change, seam_coverage, what_next — runs unchanged over an assembled view of N designs, and a WRITE made through the view lands in the design that owns the node, so there is nothing to merge back and nothing to release but the view itself. compose_and_analyse already does the read half for one pair (namespaced, writes nothing); the view generalises it to N and adds write routing.

WHERE IT IS SMALLER THAN IT SOUNDS, kept beside it: (1) it is NOT a cache — a copy would be the stored union set aside the same day; it is N open stores read through one namespaced key space, so "release" costs nothing and nothing can go stale. (2) Ids collide across designs (every design has proj:, req:a-..., who:ajs), so the view is namespaced by graph_id as compose_and_analyse already is, and every tool reply through the view carries the owning design on each id. (3) A write of an EDGE between two designs' nodes has two possible owners; the 2026-10-07 settlement already answers it — the link record lives in the design that makes it (dec:idea-a-relation-between-nodes-in-two-designs-is-recorded-so-linking-works-on-the-one-design) — and the view must apply that rule, not invent a third place. (4) Permission is per write as well as per read: a member who may read design B may not be allowed to write it through the view, and the refusal must name the design. (5) Derived scans memoised per design (detect_gaps, defects) have to be either recomputed over the view or composed from per-design results; the second is cheaper and already how compose_and_analyse works. (6) What is genuinely new is not the federation (a database view over N schemas is old) but that the design tools run over it unchanged and that a hub then holds NO copy of any member — which retires the stale-copy problem the hub has lived with since 10-04 (its watch suspended, external_dependency pins owed) at the root. This is the consumer-side payoff integrated-flo's hub work would take; the primitive stays here. Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_019Xbw6PG9mXJiU2Sb421fnq
properties.name: SETTLED 2026-10-10 — cross-design operations are one layer in the registry, taken by graph_id over the designs one process holds, with the host passing who may read what (a); RocksDB checkpoints, SST ingestion and a shared block cache are researched as later speed-ups (c); one RocksDB with a column family per design stays considered (b)
